title: Disassembly and Control Flow: From Bytes to a Graph You Can Check

questions.question: A disassembly listing from llvm-objdump shows every byte of a function decoded into real mnemonics. What does that prove?
options: That the function has no indirect jumps
That every instruction in the listing executes
That the control-flow graph is complete
Only that a linear sweep found an instruction boundary for every byte, which can still be wrong where data sits inside the code
questions.explanation: A sweep decodes data as code and re-synchronises within a few bytes, so a plausible listing is not proof of the instruction boundaries or of reachability.

questions.question: The bytes 48 8d 0d 00 00 00 00 decode to leaq (%rip), %rcx and .rela.text holds R_X86_64_PC32 .rodata-0x4 at the displacement field. Where does the operand point after linking?
options: .rodata+0x0, because the processor adds the field to the next instruction address, which is 4 bytes past the field
.rodata-0x4
The address of the lea itself
.rodata+0x4
questions.explanation: R_X86_64_PC32 stores S + A - P. The field is the last 4 bytes of the instruction, so the final target is S + A + 4 = .rodata + 0.

questions.question: In the trap fixture the table bytes are 31 c0 90 48 and the next real instruction is 83 c0 01 (addl $1, %eax). What does a linear sweep print at the jump target 0x14?
options: A nop at 0x14
An invalid opcode error at 0x13
addl $0x1, %eax at 0x14
Nothing starts at 0x14. The 48 at 0x13 becomes a REX prefix and the sweep prints addq $0x1, %rax spanning 0x13 to 0x17
questions.explanation: The REX byte joins the three bytes of the real add, so the listing shows a 64-bit add one byte early and no instruction at the branch target.

questions.question: Recursive descent over grade at -O0 stops at jmpq *%rax and reports three blocks. What evidence lets it continue to the four case blocks?
options: The bytes of the table in .rodata, which are all zero in the object file
The function size in the symbol table
The lea relocation that names the table, the cmp or sub plus ja that bounds the index, and the five R_X86_64_PC32 entries in .rela.rodata that give target = addend - 4k
The order of the blocks in the listing
questions.explanation: In a relocatable object the table holds placeholders. The relocations on the table entries are the only source of the targets, and the bounds check gives the entry count.

questions.question: Why does the iterative dominator algorithm of Cooper, Harvey, and Kennedy process blocks in reverse postorder?
options: Because the entry block must be processed last
So that most predecessors of a block already have an immediate dominator when the block is visited, which lets the fixpoint converge in few passes
Because it removes the need for the intersect step
Because reverse postorder is the order of addresses in memory
questions.explanation: Reverse postorder visits a block after its forward predecessors, so each pass propagates dominators along forward edges and only back edges need another pass.

questions.question: At -O1 clang compiles grade to cmpl $4, %ecx; ja; leaq (%rip), %rcx with a relocation to .rodata; movl (%rcx,%rax,4), %eax; retq. What should the analysis report?
options: A call through the table
A value table at .rodata+0x14 holding 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, three basic blocks, and no indirect transfer
An unresolved indirect jump
A jump table with five code targets
questions.explanation: The load is a plain movl and the function returns right after it. The optimizer replaced the case blocks with a table of return values, which changes a load and not the control flow.
